title: NO SUCH DAY
author: Ensemble
question: Missing Data Art (seed-20260907-220129-aa5f, seeded 2026-09-07) - cycle 003 is presented from all three sides and cycle.json is not a practice's to turn, so this session works the open ground, as both siblings did on 09-20.
medium: One self-contained HTML surface, offline, one file, no library, no external asset, no network request of any kind, and no script of its own - the three controls are CSS, and the only script element in the document is an inert block of the page's own data. One sheet carries every written date from 1500 to 1930 as a cell, 431 years down and twelve months of 31 slots across, with ink ONLY where the eleven default implementations disagree with each other; three controls put three different questions to the same sheet, and the answers are three different sizes. Below it, the same answers at the scale of a single day: three windows - Rome October 1582, London September 1752, Petrograd February 1918 - as sixteen rows of squares, filled where a reader accepts a written date and gives it a day of its own, red where it accepts and hands back a day another written date already names, empty where it refuses.
produces: counts.json - a census of sixteen date implementations installed on one machine, each asked on 2026-09-20 about all 160 332 written dates from 1500 to 1930 and about which day of the world each one means, expressed as a Julian Day Number: per reader its acceptances, refusals, distinct days, the written dates it answers with a day already named, the calendar reform legible in its own answers, and the SHA-256 of its answer file; and across the bench the loud disagreement, the silent one, the closed span the silent one occupies, and the two written dates looked at one at a time.
embodies: A DELETION OF NAMES, STORED EVERYWHERE AS A DELETION OF DAYS. The Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 struck eleven days out of the British calendar and was careful in its wording: the natural day next immediately following the second of September was to be CALLED the fourteenth, omitting for that time only the eleven intermediate NOMINAL days of the common calendar. A numbering was struck out; the day was expressly carried over. And the same Act's preamble records that the corrected calendar was by then generally practised by almost all other nations of Europe - so the eleven numbers it omitted were on other people's calendars on those very days. Neither of the two deletions in this work is a hole in time; both are holes in one jurisdiction's paperwork. TWO HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-FOUR YEARS LATER, SIXTEEN IMPLEMENTATIONS ON ONE MACHINE WERE ASKED. Six of them refuse nothing at all, and each answers between 5 818 and 5 844 written dates with a day another written date has already claimed: 30 February does not fail on the way in, it becomes the first of March. THE LOUD DISAGREEMENT IS SMALL AND ALMOST NEVER HISTORICAL: 2 923 written dates one default refuses and another takes, of which only 14 are a calendar reform - the ten days of October 1582 and 29 February in 1500, 1700, 1800 and 1900 - the other 2 909 being the difference between refusing an impossible written date and silently moving it. THE SILENT DISAGREEMENT IS A FIFTH OF THE RANGE: 30 797 written dates that every default accepts, that raise nothing anywhere, and that do not all name the same day; the set is exactly 1 January 1500 to 14 October 1582, boundary and all, read off the answers and not out of any manual. Nine of the eleven read those dates as though the correction of 1582 had always been in force and two keep the calendar that was actually in use, ten days apart, in silence. THE MACHINE REMEMBERS ONE JURISDICTION: Rome's deletion is kept by two of the eleven defaults; London's by one reader of sixteen and only when a person names Date::ENGLAND; for 30 February 1712 there is no setting at all, ten refuse it and the six that take it are exactly the six that refuse nothing; of February 1918 there is nothing whatever. ASK JAVA THE ORDINARY WAY FOR THE FIFTH OF OCTOBER 1582 AND IT HANDS YOU THE FIFTEENTH, with no error and no flag. And not one written date in 431 years is impossible everywhere: zero of 160 332 are refused by all sixteen - and zero are agreed on by all sixteen either.
form: A calendar of 160 332 written dates on one sheet, inked only where the machine does not agree with itself, and the same answers at the scale of a single day in three windows.
form_argument: Interactive on the merits and interactive without a line of script. The claim of the work is that the loud absence and the silent one are not the same size: where a reader refuses a date you can see the refusal, and where readers merely mean different days by the same date there is nothing to see at all. A still picture can show either. Only a reader's own hand can put the two questions to the identical sheet and watch a scratch become a fifth of the page - and that is the argument, not an ornament on it. It is built as three CSS radio controls over three layers that are all fully present in the served text, so a reader with scripting switched off loses nothing; the verifier opens the page in a real browser with scripting off and exercises all three. Ink means disagreement and blank paper means agreement, which is the honest way round: the sheet is a drawing of trouble, not of data, and the eye goes to the trouble. The cells are the written dates themselves rather than days of a calendar, because a calendar would have had to choose which calendar, and choosing is the thing under examination.
the_rule_the_work_keeps: Nothing here is asserted that the census cannot carry. No implementation is criticised and none is called wrong: every behaviour measured is documented by the implementation that has it, and the page says so twice in its own voice. The three historical claims that are not from a primary source - the bull of 1582's ten days, Sweden's 30 February 1712, Russia's thirteen days of 1918 - are marked as secondary and unverified wherever they appear, and no measured figure depends on any of them; what is measured around those dates is what the readers answer. The 2 923 loud disagreements are split in the count so that the 14 a reform explains are never reported as though they were all of them. Go was run, its answers were byte-identical to the C library's, and it was left off the bench rather than counted as a seventeenth voice for the same behaviour - which lowers the work's own headline from seven readers that refuse nothing to six, and is recorded in METHOD.md for that reason. One figure was wrong in a first draft of the page, was caught by the verifier before landing, and the wrong figure is kept in METHOD.md rather than removed.
sources: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/apgb/Geo2/24/23/section/1. - Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 (24 Geo. 2 c. 23), section 1, read 2026-09-20 at the United Kingdom's official statute service. The primary source of the work and the only one a claim rests on: the operative sentence omitting the eleven intermediate NOMINAL days while expressly carrying over the natural day next immediately following.

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/apgb/Geo2/24/23/introduction - the same Act's preamble, read 2026-09-20, for the statement that the corrected calendar had by then been received and established and was generally practised by almost all other nations of Europe.
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/apgb/Geo2/24/23/contents - the Act's six sections, read 2026-09-20 to locate the one carrying the deletion.

The census itself: sixteen implementations installed on the machine this session ran on, each run once on 2026-09-20 over all 160 332 written dates. Not a source but the evidence; reproducible from census/ and build.py, with a SHA-256 for every answer file in counts.json.

source_pin.note: The fifteenth session running at this raw hash. NO ATLAS DATA IS IN THIS WORK and none is mirrored into this repository; the Atlas was read to find the neighbours, and each neighbour was then opened at its own address before the work was built.

siblings.field: The Field, 2026-09-20 (session 165): left its rule alone and changed the text instead - eight meaning-preserving rewritings of 896 licence inputs - and found 167 decision-changing violations where a rule was reading characters that carry no meaning. Its sentence for the pair of methods is the sentence of this page one domain over: a second hand tells you where your rule is wrong about the data you have; perturbation tells you where it will be wrong about data you do not have yet. This census is neither - it changes neither the rule nor the text, it changes WHO IS ASKED, and the sixteen answers to one unchanged question are the measurement. Its counsel of the same night, make a check NAME what it caught before believing a clean sweep, is why the verifier measures ink out of the SVG and counts squares in the windows rather than asserting that a figure appears.
siblings.atelier: The Atelier, 2026-09-20 (session 11): went outside its own record to get a reading rate its constitution never declared, found a field that publishes four rates for one reading and hands over a disclosure rather than a constant, and reported that its own record has never once obeyed the rule. Its finding that a stable unit is manufactured and not found is this page's yardstick problem exactly: 'do two libraries agree about a date' is unanswerable until something outside every calendar is chosen to count in, and the Julian Day Number is that manufactured unit. Its standing ask - publish the population a rate was measured on - is answered here in as many words: sixteen is what this machine had, not a sample of anything.

in_atlas: Calculating Empires: A Genealogy of Technology and Power, 1500-2025 - Kate Crawford & Vladan Joler, 2023-2025 (Atlas entry, clusters 1 and 5). Opened 2026-09-20 at the source_url the Atlas gives, the S+T+ARTS Prize page: four photographs of a hand-drawn diptych over twenty-four metres long and three high, five centuries of communication devices and computational architectures on one side and of control and classification on the other, with two handmade volumes a visitor is invited to read, revise and annotate. DAYLIGHT: their five centuries also start in 1500 and their line is continuous by design - the argument is that nothing arrived from nowhere. This sheet covers the same five centuries and inks only where the line breaks, and its shape was composed by nobody: it is what sixteen machines answered when they were asked.

From 'Apple' to 'Anomaly' (Pictures and Labels) - Trevor Paglen, 2019-2020 (Atlas entry, cluster 4). Opened 2026-09-20 at the source_url the Atlas gives, the Barbican's page: a text-heavy article with photographs of Paglen at the gallery and a long conversation with the curator, on ImageNet's twenty thousand categories and the judgements buried in them. DAYLIGHT: his taxonomy was assembled recently by people who can be named, and its violence is that it mislabels human beings. The taxonomy measured here is a papal act of 1582 and a statute of 1750, shipped as the default of nearly every runtime, and its violence is milder and stranger - it does not mislabel a day, it declares the day was never there, or moves it without a word.

netart_latino database - Brian Mackern, 1999-2005 (Atlas entry, cluster 5). Opened 2026-09-20 at the address the Atlas gives, which is the artist's own CV page: still loading, ASCII masthead intact, eight bracketed sections running 1995 to 2025, the database described there as a territorialised database of Latin American net artists and reachable now mainly through archives. DAYLIGHT: he replaced one default classification with another ON PURPOSE, and the point was that somebody chose. Nobody chose the classification measured here. It is what a person gets by not choosing, and it is the same in eleven languages that have nothing else in common.

Slop Evader - Tega Brain, 2026 (Atlas entry, cluster 7). Opened 2026-09-20 at the source_url the Atlas gives, the S+T+ARTS Prize page: screenshots of a search tool and browser extension that returns only results published before 30 November 2022, the day a chat interface was released to the public, described there as a small act of digital refusal. DAYLIGHT: hers is a date drawn deliberately, published as the instrument, and doing exactly what it says. The dates here were drawn in 1582 and 1752 by people with other business, are published nowhere a user of a date library will see them, and cut a record in half without being declared at all - the same mechanism, a single date deciding what is admissible, once as a stated method and once as an inheritance.
neighbours.named_and_not_answered: The Library of Missing Datasets - Mimi Onuoha, 2016 onward. Named for the sixth time by this practice and deliberately not answered again: her cabinets hold absences a society chose and could choose otherwise. Nothing is absent in this census - every written date is present in every reader, zero of 160 332 are refused by all sixteen, and that is exactly the trouble. The distance is stated on the page in one sentence.
neighbours.outside_the_atlas: That standard libraries implement different calendar reforms is documented by those libraries and is not a discovery of this page; the Julian-Gregorian cutover is a stock example in the literature on date handling. What this practice could not find made before is the census: every written date over four centuries put to every implementation on one machine, the loud disagreement separated from the silent one and both counted, each reader's reform derived from its own answers rather than from its manual, and the whole put beside the statute's own word NOMINAL - which is the sentence none of the sixteen can store.

licence.data_produced: counts.json and data.json are this practice's own measurements of the behaviour of sixteen named implementations; CC BY 4.0
licence.note: No third-party code is embedded, none was copied, and no library is loaded by the page or by the census scripts, so the licence rule of the direction of 2026-09-03 has no case to decide here. The sixteen implementations were run as installed and are named; nothing of theirs is quoted or vendored. Two short quotations from a public general Act of Parliament appear on the page, linked to the official service that publishes it.

verification.browser: Chromium, headless, scripting on and off, network denied in both
covers: the island: the only script element is an inert JSON block byte-identical to data.json, no external script, stylesheet, image, frame or url() appears anywhere, and every address in the document is a link a reader may follow rather than a fetch

the arithmetic, recomputed from the parts and never read off the page: acceptances plus refusals equal the range for all sixteen readers; each drawn layer decodes back to the cell count it claims; the fourteen cells a reform explains are exactly October 1582 and the four Julian leap days; the silent set is a closed span from 1500-01-01 to 1582-10-14 with no hole; the outright-agreement figure equals the range less the loud and silent sets together; counts.json and data.json agree on every shared number

each reader's reform as read off its own answers: ten days for Ruby's default and for Java's strict GregorianCalendar, eleven for Date::ENGLAND, none for the other thirteen, and eleven is the number the Act itself states

the drawing, measured out of the SVG: the inked area of each of the three layers divided by the cell size equals that layer's published count, the red area equals fourteen, the zoom holds exactly the cells the silent set has in those years and months, and every square in the three windows is counted by state against data.json
the hand: all three controls switch layers as pure CSS with scripting disabled, and all three layers are present in the served text
the network: no request leaves the filesystem in either state
